items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, governs the taxation of income in India, including the taxation of business expenses. Section 37 of the Act allows businesses to deduct expenses that are wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business, unless otherwise specifically disallowed. However, the allowability of certain expenses, such as those related to patent settlements, can be contentious. The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has issued various circulars and guidelines to clarify the allowability of such expenses, including Circular No. 5/2015, which provides guidance on the allowability of expenditure on scientific research. Furthermore, Section 145A of the Income Tax Act provides for the valuation of inventory and the allowability of certain expenditures.

In the context of transfer pricing, Section 92 of the Income Tax Act requires that international transactions between associated enterprises be conducted at arm's length. The CBDT has issued various guidelines and regulations to implement these provisions, including the Transfer Pricing Regulations, 2001. The Regulations provide for the computation of arm's length price and the allowability of certain adjustments. The ITAT has also issued several rulings on transfer pricing, including the ruling in the case of LG Electronics India Pvt. Ltd. vs. DCIT, which provides guidance on the allowability of captive power adjustments.

The Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime, introduced in 2017, also has implications for the taxation of business expenses. Section 16 of the CGST Act, 2017, provides for the eligibility and conditions for taking input tax credit, while Section 17(5) of the Act disallows input tax credit on certain expenses, including those related to entertainment and club memberships. The CBIC has issued various circulars and guidelines to clarify the allowability of input tax credit on certain expenses, including Circular No. 102/21/2019, which provides guidance on the allowability of input tax credit on expenses related to employee benefits.

Facts of the Case

The present case involves Sun Pharma, a pharmaceutical company, which had incurred a patent settlement expense of ₹602 crore. The company had claimed this expense as a deductible business expense under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. However, the Assessing Officer (AO) had disallowed this expense, holding that it was not wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business. The AO had also made a transfer pricing adjustment, disallowing the captive power adjustment claimed by the company. The company had appealed against this order before the ITAT.

The company had also claimed a disallowance under Section 14A of the Income Tax Act, which provides for the disallowance of expenditure incurred in relation to income that is exempt from tax. The AO had restricted this disallowance to the dividend earned by the company, but the company had argued that this restriction was not justified. The ITAT had to examine the allowability of the patent settlement expense, the captive power adjustment, and the disallowance under Section 14A.

The company had also relied on various judicial precedents, including the ruling of the Supreme Court in the case of India Cine Agencies vs. CIT, which provides guidance on the allowability of business expenses. The company had argued that the patent settlement expense was a genuine business expense, incurred to settle a dispute related to a patent, and was therefore allowable as a deductible business expense.

Issue Before the Tribunal

The issue before the ITAT was whether the patent settlement expense of ₹602 crore was allowable as a deductible business expense under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. The ITAT also had to examine the allowability of the captive power adjustment and the disallowance under Section 14A. The company had argued that the patent settlement expense was a genuine business expense, incurred to settle a dispute related to a patent, and was therefore allowable as a deductible business expense.

The ITAT had to consider the provisions of Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, which allows businesses to deduct expenses that are wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business. The ITAT also had to consider the provisions of Section 145A of the Income Tax Act, which provides for the valuation of inventory and the allowability of certain expenditures. The ITAT had to examine the facts of the case and the applicable law to determine the allowability of the patent settlement expense and the other expenses claimed by the company.

The ITAT's decision would have significant implications for the company and for other businesses that incur similar expenses. The decision would provide guidance on the allowability of patent settlement expenses and other business expenses, and would help to clarify the application of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act. The decision would also be relevant to the GST regime, as it would provide guidance on the allowability of input tax credit on certain expenses.

Arguments & Contentions

The company had argued that the patent settlement expense was a genuine business expense, incurred to settle a dispute related to a patent, and was therefore allowable as a deductible business expense. The company had relied on various judicial precedents, including the ruling of the Supreme Court in the case of India Cine Agencies vs. CIT, which provides guidance on the allowability of business expenses. The company had also argued that the captive power adjustment was allowable, as it was a genuine business expense incurred to generate power for the company's operations.

The Revenue had argued that the patent settlement expense was not wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business, and was therefore not allowable as a deductible business expense. The Revenue had also argued that the captive power adjustment was not allowable, as it was not a genuine business expense. The Revenue had relied on various provisions of the Income Tax Act, including Section 37 and Section 145A, to support its arguments.

The company had also argued that the disallowance under Section 14A should not be restricted to the dividend earned by the company. The company had argued that this restriction was not justified, as the expenditure incurred by the company was not solely related to the dividend earned. The company had relied on various judicial precedents, including the ruling of the ITAT in the case of DCIT vs. Jindal Stainless Ltd., which provides guidance on the allowability of expenditure under Section 14A.

Tribunal's Ruling & Reasoning

The ITAT allowed the patent settlement expense of ₹602 crore as a deductible business expense under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act. The ITAT held that the expense was wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business, and was therefore allowable as a deductible business expense. The ITAT also deleted the captive power adjustment, holding that it was a genuine business expense incurred to generate power for the company's operations.

The ITAT restricted the disallowance under Section 14A to the dividend earned by the company. The ITAT held that the expenditure incurred by the company was related to the dividend earned, and that the disallowance should therefore be restricted to the dividend earned. The ITAT's decision was based on a careful examination of the facts of the case and the applicable law, including the provisions of Section 37 and Section 145A of the Income Tax Act.

The ITAT's decision provides significant guidance on the allowability of patent settlement expenses and other business expenses. The decision highlights the importance of examining the facts of each case carefully, and of applying the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act in a nuanced and context-specific manner. The decision will be relevant to other businesses that incur similar expenses, and will help to clarify the application of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act.

Key Takeaways for Practitioners

Here are five key takeaways for practitioners from the ITAT's decision: 1. Patent settlement expenses can be allowable as deductible business expenses under Section 37 of the Income Tax Act, if they are wholly and exclusively incurred for the purpose of business. 2. Captive power adjustments can be allowable as genuine business expenses, if they are incurred to generate power for the company's operations. 3. Disallowances under Section 14A should be restricted to the dividend earned by the company, if the expenditure incurred by the company is related to the dividend earned. 4. Practitioners should carefully examine the facts of each case and apply the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act in a nuanced and context-specific manner, to ensure that business expenses are allowable as deductible expenses. 5. Practitioners should also consider the implications of the GST regime on the allowability of business expenses, and should ensure that input tax credit is claimed correctly on allowable expenses.

Overall, the ITAT's decision provides significant guidance on the allowability of patent settlement expenses and other business expenses, and highlights the importance of careful examination of the facts of each case and nuanced application of the relevant provisions of the Income Tax Act. Practitioners should take note of these key takeaways and apply them in their practice, to ensure that their clients receive the correct tax treatment for their business expenses.

items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The circular clarifies that the exempt amount shall be computed with reference to the amount received by the employee as a result of voluntary retirement, and not with reference to the amount received as a result of retirement under a specific scheme.

items.title: Ahmedabad ITAT Deletes On-Money Addition for Lack of Link to Assessee
items.summary: Ahmedabad ITAT deleted the section 69 on-money addition as seized material did not link the assessee to any cash payment or support the alleged amount. The post Ahmedabad ITAT Deletes On-Money Addition for Lack of Link to Assessee appeared first on TaxGuru .
items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, empowers the Assessing Officer to make additions to the total income of an assessee under various provisions, including Section 69, which deals with unexplained investments. This section is often invoked when the Assessing Officer discovers investments or expenditures that are not satisfactorily explained by the assessee. The provision is designed to curb black money and ensure that all income is accounted for and taxed accordingly. Section 69 states that if an assessee has made an investment which is not recorded in the books of account, and the assessee offers no explanation about the source of the investment, or the explanation offered is not satisfactory, the value of the investment can be treated as income of the assessee for that year.

Furthermore, the concept of "on-money" transactions, which refers to payments made in cash without being recorded in the books of account, is a common reason for invoking Section 69. The Assessing Officer must, however, establish a clear link between the assessee and the unexplained investment or cash payment. This link is crucial for sustaining an addition under Section 69, as merely seizing cash or discovering unexplained investments is not sufficient without establishing the assessee's involvement. The legal framework surrounding Section 69 is designed to ensure that additions are made based on tangible evidence and not mere suspicion or conjecture.

The CBDT has also issued guidelines and circulars to streamline the process of making additions under Section 69 and to ensure that the rights of the assessee are protected. For instance, the CBDT has emphasized the importance of conducting thorough investigations and gathering concrete evidence before making any additions. The Assessing Officer must also provide the assessee with an opportunity to explain the source of the investment or cash payment, as mandated by the principles of natural justice. This ensures that the assessee is given a fair chance to defend themselves against any allegations of unexplained investments or income.

Facts of the Case

The Ahmedabad ITAT's decision to delete the on-money addition under Section 69 is significant because it underscores the importance of establishing a direct link between the assessee and the alleged unexplained investment or cash payment. In this case, the Assessing Officer had made an addition under Section 69 based on seized material that allegedly indicated on-money transactions. However, upon closer examination, it became apparent that the seized material did not provide conclusive evidence linking the assessee to these transactions. The absence of such a link is critical, as it goes to the heart of the Assessing Officer's ability to sustain an addition under Section 69.

The facts of the case highlight the challenges faced by the Assessing Officer in establishing the nexus between the assessee and the unexplained investments or cash payments. items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

Section 148A(b) specifically requires that the assessee be given an opportunity to furnish return of income or any other information, as the case may be, within a period of at least seven days from the date of service of the notice. Furthermore, the Supreme Court and High Courts have also laid down important principles and guidelines in this regard. In the case of GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. vs. Income Tax Officer, the Supreme Court held that the provisions of Section 148A must be strictly construed, and any deviation from the procedural requirements could result in the reassessment proceedings being quashed. These judicial pronouncements have significant implications for tax practitioners and assessees, highlighting the need for strict adherence to the procedural requirements under the Act.

Facts of the Case

The present case involves a reassessment notice issued by the Assessing Officer under Section 148A of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The notice was served on the assessee, granting less than the mandatory seven days' time to respond. The ITAT considered the facts of the case, including the date of service of the notice and the time granted to the assessee to respond. The Tribunal also examined the provisions of Section 148A and the relevant circulars and guidelines issued by the CBDT. Arguments & Contentions

The ITAT considered the arguments and contentions of both parties, examining the provisions of Section 148A and the relevant circulars and guidelines issued by the CBDT. Tribunal's Ruling & Reasoning

The ITAT held that the reassessment notice issued under Section 148A was invalid, as it did not comply with the mandatory requirement of granting at least seven days' time to the assessee to respond. The Tribunal relied on the provisions of Section 148A(b) and the relevant circulars and guidelines issued by the CBDT, which emphasize the importance of adhering to the time limits and procedural requirements prescribed under the Act.

The ITAT also relied on judicial pronouncements, including the decision in GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. vs. Income Tax Officer, which held that the provisions of Section 148A must be strictly construed. The Tribunal held that the revenue authorities had failed to comply with the procedural requirements under Section 148A(b), which had resulted in the notice being invalid.

The ITAT's ruling in this case is significant, as it reiterates the importance of adhering to the procedural requirements under the Act. The Tribunal's decision has implications for tax practitioners, assessees, and revenue authorities, highlighting the need for careful attention to the time limits and procedural requirements prescribed under the Act. Key Takeaways for Practitioners

items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, provides the framework for the assessment of income tax in India. Section 143(2) of the Act is a critical provision that deals with the issuance of notices by the Assessing Officer (AO) to the taxpayer, requiring them to attend the assessment proceedings. This notice is a prerequisite for a valid assessment, as it informs the taxpayer of the intention to assess their income and provides an opportunity to present their case. The AO's jurisdiction is defined under Section 124 of the Act, which outlines the territorial areas within which an AO can exercise their powers.

In the context of a change in jurisdiction, Section 127 of the Act empowers the Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) to transfer cases from one AO to another. However, this transfer must be accompanied by a fresh notice under Section 143(2) to ensure that the taxpayer is aware of the change in jurisdiction and the new AO's intention to assess their income. The CBDT has also issued circulars, such as Circular No. 14/2015, which provide guidance on the procedure to be followed in cases of transfer of jurisdiction.

The significance of a fresh Section 143(2) notice after a change in jurisdiction cannot be overstated. It is a fundamental principle of natural justice that the taxpayer must be given an opportunity to be heard before an adverse decision is made against them. The issuance of a fresh notice ensures that the taxpayer is aware of the new AO's intention to assess their income and provides an opportunity to present their case, thereby upholding the principles of fairness and transparency.

Facts of the Case

The case before the Delhi ITAT involved a change in jurisdiction, where the original AO's jurisdiction was transferred to a new AO. The taxpayer challenged the assessment on the grounds that the new AO had not issued a fresh notice under Section 143(2) after the change in jurisdiction, which is a mandatory requirement under the Act. The taxpayer argued that the assessment was therefore invalid and should be quashed. ITO, which highlights the importance of issuing a notice under Section 143(2) before making an assessment. The Revenue, on the other hand, argued that the assessment made by the new AO was valid, as the original notice under Section 143(2) issued by the previous AO was still in force. Tribunal's Ruling & Reasoning

The ITAT ruled in favor of the taxpayer, holding that the assessment made by the new AO was invalid due to the failure to issue a fresh notice under Section 143(2) after the change in jurisdiction. The Tribunal held that the failure to issue a fresh notice under Section 143(2) after the change in jurisdiction was a fatal flaw that rendered the assessment invalid.

The ITAT's ruling has significant implications for taxpayers and AOs alike. The ITAT's ruling also emphasizes the need for AOs to issue fresh notices under Section 143(2) after a change in jurisdiction to ensure that assessments are valid and not prone to challenge.

Key Takeaways for Practitioners

The ITAT's ruling in this case provides important guidance for taxpayers and practitioners. The following are some key takeaways from the decision:

items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, contains various provisions to counter tax evasion and ensure that taxpayers do not inflate their expenses to reduce their taxable income. One such provision is Section 69C, which deals with unexplained expenditures or investments that are deemed to be the income of the taxpayer. This section is particularly relevant in cases where the assessing officer suspects that a taxpayer has made bogus purchases to reduce their taxable income. The Delhi ITAT's recent judgment, restricting the Section 69C bogus purchase addition to 6% where sales were accepted, is a significant development in this context.

Section 69C of the Income Tax Act states that where any taxpayer has made an expenditure or incurred an expense, and the assessing officer is of the opinion that such expenditure or expense is not genuine, then the assessing officer may treat such expenditure or expense as the income of the taxpayer. This provision is aimed at preventing taxpayers from making false claims of expenses to reduce their taxable income. In conjunction with Section 145A, which deals with the method of accounting, the assessing officer can make adjustments to the taxpayer's income to reflect the true financial position.

The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has also issued circulars and guidelines to clarify the application of Section 69C. For instance, the CBDT has emphasized the importance of verifying the genuineness of transactions and ensuring that the addition made under Section 69C is based on credible evidence. The CBDT has also cautioned against making additions without proper investigation and verification of facts. In the context of the Delhi ITAT's judgment, it is essential to consider the interplay between Section 69C and other provisions of the Income Tax Act, such as Section 37, which deals with business expenses.

Facts of the Case

The assessing officer had made an addition under Section 69C of the Income Tax Act, treating a certain amount as bogus purchases. The taxpayer had claimed that the purchases were genuine and supported by documentary evidence. However, the assessing officer was not satisfied with the explanation and made the addition. The taxpayer appealed against the order, arguing that the addition was not justified and that the sales corresponding to the alleged bogus purchases had been accepted by the department.

The taxpayer submitted that the assessing officer had not properly appreciated the facts of the case and had failed to consider the evidence on record. The taxpayer relied on various judgments, including those of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, to support their contention that the addition was not justified. The ITAT also observed that the sales corresponding to the alleged bogus purchases had been accepted by the department. In this context, the ITAT applied the principles laid down in the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Durga Chambers, which deals with the principles of natural justice and the importance of considering the evidence on record.

Issue Before the Tribunal

The primary issue before the ITAT was whether the addition made under Section 69C was justified, given that the sales corresponding to the alleged bogus purchases had been accepted by the department. The ITAT had to consider whether the assessing officer had properly appreciated the facts of the case and had followed the principles of natural justice. The ITAT had to weigh the evidence on record and consider the arguments advanced by the taxpayer. The ITAT also had to consider the judgments of the Supreme Court and the High Courts, which have laid down the principles for making additions under Section 69C. In this context, the ITAT applied the principles laid down in the judgment of the Delhi High Court in the case of Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Suresh Kumar Aggarwal, which deals with the principles of making additions under Section 69C.

The ITAT's decision would have significant implications for taxpayers who have made similar claims of bogus purchases. The judgment would provide guidance on the application of Section 69C and the principles to be followed by the assessing officer when making additions under this provision. items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, provides for the assessment of income that has escaped assessment or has been under-assessed. Section 153C of the Act is a special provision for assessment of income of any other person, wherein the Assessing Officer can assess the income of any person other than the person searched, if such income is found to be related to the person searched. However, such assessment can only be made if the Assessing Officer is satisfied that any money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable article or thing, or any income based on any entry or entries in the books of account or other documents, seized or requisitioned, belongs to the other person. Furthermore, Section 69A of the Act provides for the assessment of unexplained money, etc., wherein if in any financial year, the assessee is found to be the owner of any money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable article, and such money, bullion, jewellery, or other valuable article is not recorded in the books of account, the same shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee for that financial year.

It is crucial to understand the statutory framework and the intent behind these provisions. Section 153C is aimed at bringing to tax the income that has escaped assessment, while Section 69A is aimed at taxing the unexplained money or assets found with the assessee. The Assessing Officer must follow the due process of law and ensure that the additions made are based on incriminating material. The concept of incriminating material is crucial, as it provides the link between the seized material and the income that has escaped assessment. The absence of such material can render the assessment proceedings bad in law.

The CBDT has also issued various circulars and guidelines to ensure that the Assessing Officers follow the due process of law while making assessments under Section 153C. For instance, the CBDT has clarified that the Assessing Officer must record his satisfaction in writing before making an assessment under Section 153C. This clarification is essential to ensure that the Assessing Officer has applied his mind to the facts of the case and has formed a reasonable belief that the income belongs to the person other than the person searched.

Facts of the Case

The Delhi ITAT recently had the opportunity to decide on an appeal filed by the revenue against an order of the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), wherein the Commissioner had deleted the addition made under Section 69A of the Act. The Tribunal's decision is significant, as it highlights the importance of following the due process of law in assessment proceedings. The assessee, on the other hand, argued that the unsecured loans were genuinely recorded in the regular books of account, and that there was no incriminating material to suggest that the loans were not genuine. The assessee contended that the Assessing Officer had not followed the due process of law in making the assessment under Section 153C, and that the addition made under Section 69A of the Act was therefore bad in law.

The arguments and contentions of the parties are significant, as they highlight the conflicting views on the interpretation of the provisions of the Act. The revenue's argument is based on the assumption that the unsecured loans were not recorded in the regular books of account, while the assessee's argument is based on the fact that the loans were genuinely recorded in the regular books of account. Tribunal's Ruling & Reasoning

Key Takeaways for Practitioners

items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, empowers the Assessing Officer (AO) to reassess income that has escaped assessment under Section 147. However, this power is not unfettered and is subject to certain conditions and safeguards. One such safeguard is the requirement of obtaining prior approval from the specified authority under Section 151 before issuing a notice under Section 148 for reopening an assessment. The purpose of this approval is to ensure that the reopening of an assessment is not done mechanically or without due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case.

Section 151 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, mandates that the AO shall not issue a notice under Section 148 unless he has obtained the prior approval of the Joint Commissioner or the Assistant Commissioner or the Deputy Commissioner, as the case may be. This approval is a critical check to prevent arbitrary or unjustified reopening of assessments. The CBDT has also issued guidelines and circulars emphasizing the importance of this approval and the need for a thorough examination of the grounds for reopening before granting such approval.

The Supreme Court and various High Courts have also underscored the significance of this approval in several judgments, including the landmark case of GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. vs. Income Tax Officer, where it was held that the approval under Section 151 is a condition precedent for issuing a notice under Section 148. Therefore, any mechanical or invalid approval can render the subsequent reassessment proceedings without legal basis.

Facts of the Case

In the instant case, the AO issued a notice under Section 148 to the taxpayer for reopening an assessment that had already been completed. The taxpayer challenged this notice on the grounds that the approval granted under Section 151 was mechanical and did not consider the merits of the case. The taxpayer contended that the approval was merely a formality and did not satisfy the legal requirements under Section 151.

The AO, on the other hand, argued that the approval was granted after due consideration of the facts and that the taxpayer had failed to demonstrate any error or illegality in the approval process. The AO relied on the provisions of Section 151 and the CBDT's guidelines to support his contention that the approval was valid and in accordance with the law.

The dispute ultimately reached the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT), which was required to adjudicate on the validity of the approval under Section 151 and its impact on the reassessment proceedings. The ITAT had to consider the legal framework, the facts of the case, and the arguments advanced by both parties to determine whether the approval was indeed mechanical and invalid.

Issue Before the Tribunal

The primary issue before the ITAT was whether the approval granted under Section 151 was mechanical and invalid, thereby rendering the notice under Section 148 and the subsequent reassessment proceedings without legal basis. The ITAT had to examine the approval process, the grounds for reopening, and the application of Section 151 to determine the validity of the approval.

The ITAT also had to consider the implications of a mechanical approval on the rights of the taxpayer and the rule of law. The tribunal was required to balance the need for the AO to reassess income that may have escaped taxation with the need to protect the taxpayer from arbitrary or unjustified actions by the revenue authorities.

The ITAT's decision would have significant implications for the taxpayer, the revenue authorities, and the broader community of taxpayers and practitioners. It would provide clarity on the requirements for a valid approval under Section 151 and the consequences of a mechanical or invalid approval on reassessment proceedings.

Arguments & Contentions

The taxpayer argued that the approval under Section 151 was granted without due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. The taxpayer contended that the approval was a mere formality and did not satisfy the legal requirements under Section 151. The taxpayer relied on the CBDT's guidelines and judicial precedents to support his contention that the approval was invalid.

The AO, on the other hand, argued that the approval was granted after a thorough examination of the grounds for reopening and that the taxpayer had failed to demonstrate any error or illegality in the approval process. The AO relied on the provisions of Section 151 and the CBDT's guidelines to support his contention that the approval was valid and in accordance with the law.

The ITAT considered the arguments and contentions of both parties, examined the approval process, and applied the relevant legal provisions to determine the validity of the approval. The tribunal's decision would be based on a thorough analysis of the facts, the law, and the circumstances of the case.

Tribunal's Ruling & Reasoning

The ITAT held that the approval granted under Section 151 was indeed mechanical and invalid. The tribunal found that the approval did not satisfy the legal requirements under Section 151 and that the AO had failed to demonstrate that the approval was granted after due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case.

The ITAT relied on the provisions of Section 151, the CBDT's guidelines, and judicial precedents to support its decision. The tribunal held that the approval was a mere formality and did not meet the requirements of a valid approval under Section 151. The ITAT quashed the reassessment proceedings, holding that the notice under Section 148 was without legal basis due to the invalid approval.

The ITAT's decision underscores the importance of a valid approval under Section 151 for reassessment proceedings. The tribunal's ruling emphasizes that the approval cannot be a mere formality and must be granted after due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. The decision provides clarity on the requirements for a valid approval and the consequences of a mechanical or invalid approval on reassessment proceedings.

Key Takeaways for Practitioners

The ITAT's decision has significant implications for practitioners, including Chartered Accountants and tax lawyers. The following are key takeaways from the decision:

1. Ensure due diligence in obtaining approval under Section 151: Practitioners should ensure that the approval under Section 151 is granted after due consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. A mechanical or invalid approval can render the reassessment proceedings without legal basis.

2. Verify the approval process: Practitioners should verify that the approval process under Section 151 is in accordance with the law and the CBDT's guidelines. This includes ensuring that the approval is granted by the competent authority and that the grounds for reopening are properly considered.

3. Challenge invalid approvals: Practitioners should challenge any invalid or mechanical approvals under Section 151. This can be done by filing an appeal before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) or the ITAT, as the case may be.

4. Maintain detailed documentation: Practitioners should maintain detailed documentation of the approval process under Section 151, including the grounds for reopening, the approval granted, and any subsequent correspondence with the revenue authorities. This documentation can be crucial in challenging any invalid or mechanical approvals.

5. This can help ensure that the taxpayer's rights are protected and that the reassessment proceedings are conducted in accordance with the law.

Background & Statutory Framework

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been at the forefront of implementing Basel norms in the Indian banking sector. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS) had introduced the Basel III framework, which includes three pillars: Pillar 1 (minimum capital requirements), Pillar 2 (supervisory review and evaluation process), and Pillar 3 (market discipline through disclosure requirements). In India, the RBI has been implementing these norms through various circulars and guidelines. Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, empowers the RBI to issue directions to banks, which includes the power to regulate their disclosure requirements. The RBI's Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026, revising the Basel Pillar 3 disclosure norms, is a significant development in this regard.

The Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements are aimed at promoting market discipline by requiring banks to disclose their risk management practices, capital adequacy, and other relevant information. This enables stakeholders, including investors and depositors, to make informed decisions. In India, the RBI has been gradually implementing the Basel III framework, with a focus on strengthening the banking sector's capital adequacy and risk management practices. The revision of the Basel Pillar 3 disclosure norms is a crucial step in this direction. As per Section 45W of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the RBI is required to regulate the banking system to ensure its stability and soundness.

The RBI's guidelines on Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements are issued under the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. These guidelines require commercial banks to disclose their risk management practices, capital adequacy, and other relevant information on a regular basis. The revision of these guidelines, as announced in the Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026, is expected to enhance the transparency and accountability of commercial banks in India. The CBDT's circulars, such as Circular No. 15/2015, have also emphasized the importance of transparency and disclosure in the banking sector.

The Development in Detail

The Seventh Amendment Directions, 2026, issued by the RBI, revise the Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements for commercial banks in India. The revised guidelines will come into effect from April 1, 2027, with a phased reporting schedule starting from June 2027. The revised guidelines aim to enhance the transparency and accountability of commercial banks by requiring them to disclose more detailed information about their risk management practices, capital adequacy, and other relevant information. The RBI has also introduced new disclosure requirements, such as the disclosure of leverage ratio and liquidity coverage ratio, to align with international best practices.

The revised guidelines require commercial banks to disclose their risk management practices, including their risk assessment and mitigation strategies, on a quarterly basis. The banks will also be required to disclose their capital adequacy, including their common equity tier 1 (CET1) capital, tier 1 capital, and total capital, on a quarterly basis. The revised guidelines also require banks to disclose their leverage ratio, liquidity coverage ratio, and net stable funding ratio on a quarterly basis. The RBI has also introduced new templates for disclosure, which will enable banks to provide more detailed and standardized information to stakeholders.

The phased reporting schedule, starting from June 2027, will enable commercial banks to gradually transition to the revised disclosure requirements. The RBI has also provided guidance on the implementation of the revised guidelines, including the requirements for data collection, validation, and verification. The revised guidelines are expected to enhance the transparency and accountability of commercial banks, which will enable stakeholders to make more informed decisions. As per Section 45W of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the RBI is required to regulate the banking system to ensure its stability and soundness, and the revised guidelines are a step in this direction.

Key Provisions & Impact

The revised guidelines will have a significant impact on the banking sector, as they will require banks to invest in new systems and processes to collect, validate, and verify the required data. However, banks will need to ensure that they have the necessary infrastructure and resources in place to comply with the revised guidelines. The RBI's guidelines on Basel Pillar 3 disclosure requirements are issued under the powers conferred by Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and non-compliance with these guidelines can result in penalties and fines.

The revised guidelines will also have implications for the Indian economy, as they will enhance the stability and soundness of the banking sector. A stable and sound banking sector is essential for the overall health of the economy, as it enables the efficient allocation of resources and facilitates economic growth. A stable and sound banking sector is essential for the overall health of the economy, as it enables the efficient allocation of resources and facilitates economic growth. Compliance Implications & Action Points

Banks will need to ensure that they have the necessary infrastructure and resources in place to comply with the revised guidelines. The following are key takeaways for practitioners:

items.title: RBI Amends Commercial Bank Asset Liability Management Directions for LCR and NSFR Disclosures from April 1, 2027

items.body:
Background & Statutory Framework

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) plays a crucial role in regulating and supervising commercial banks in India, ensuring their stability and soundness. One of the key aspects of this regulation is the management of asset liability by commercial banks, which is critical for maintaining their liquidity and solvency. The RBI has been empowered to regulate and supervise commercial banks under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. Specifically, Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, empowers the RBI to issue directions to commercial banks on various matters, including asset liability management.

The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) are two important metrics used to assess the liquidity and stability of commercial banks. The LCR is a measure of a bank's ability to meet its short-term liquidity needs, while the NSFR is a measure of a bank's ability to fund its activities over a one-year horizon. The RBI has been monitoring these ratios closely and has been issuing guidelines and directions to commercial banks to ensure that they maintain adequate liquidity and stability. For instance, the RBI's Master Circular on Liquidity Risk Management, which is updated annually, provides detailed guidelines on the management of liquidity risk by commercial banks.

The RBI's regulatory framework for commercial banks is also complemented by the guidelines and standards issued by international regulatory bodies, such as the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). The BCBS has issued guidelines on liquidity risk management, including the LCR and NSFR, which have been adopted by the RBI and incorporated into its regulatory framework. For example, the RBI's guidelines on LCR and NSFR are broadly in line with the BCBS's guidelines on these ratios, and the RBI has been working to ensure that Indian commercial banks are compliant with these international standards.

The Development in Detail

The RBI's Second Amendment Directions, 2026, which revise the LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements for commercial banks, are a significant development in this context. These directions, which will come into effect from April 1, 2027, aim to enhance the transparency and comparability of the LCR and NSFR disclosures made by commercial banks. The revised directions require commercial banks to disclose their LCR and NSFR on a quarterly basis, with effect from the quarter ending June 30, 2027. This will enable the RBI and other stakeholders to monitor the liquidity and stability of commercial banks more closely and take timely corrective action, if necessary.

The revised directions also specify the format and content of the LCR and NSFR disclosures, which will help to ensure consistency and comparability across commercial banks. For example, the disclosures will need to include the bank's LCR and NSFR, as well as a breakdown of the components of these ratios, such as high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) and total net cash outflows. This will provide stakeholders with a more detailed understanding of the bank's liquidity and funding profile and enable them to make more informed decisions.

The RBI's decision to revise the LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements is also in line with international best practices and standards. The BCBS has emphasized the importance of transparency and comparability in liquidity risk management, and the RBI's revised directions are consistent with these guidelines. By enhancing the transparency and comparability of LCR and NSFR disclosures, the RBI is helping to promote a more stable and resilient banking system in India.

Key Provisions & Impact

The revised LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements will have a significant impact on commercial banks in India. The quarterly disclosure requirement will enable the RBI to monitor the liquidity and stability of commercial banks more closely and take timely corrective action, if necessary. This will help to prevent liquidity crises and promote a more stable banking system. For example, if a commercial bank's LCR or NSFR is below the prescribed threshold, the RBI can take prompt action to require the bank to take remedial measures, such as increasing its HQLA or reducing its total net cash outflows.

The revised directions will also enhance the transparency and accountability of commercial banks, as they will be required to disclose their LCR and NSFR on a regular basis. This will enable stakeholders, including depositors and investors, to make more informed decisions about their dealings with commercial banks. For instance, a depositor may choose to deposit their funds with a bank that has a higher LCR or NSFR, as this may indicate a lower risk of liquidity problems.

The revised directions may also have implications for the risk management practices of commercial banks. The enhanced disclosure requirements may encourage commercial banks to adopt more robust risk management practices, such as more sophisticated liquidity risk management systems and more effective funding strategies. This, in turn, may help to promote a more stable and resilient banking system in India. For example, a commercial bank may choose to implement a more advanced liquidity risk management system, which can help to identify and mitigate potential liquidity risks more effectively.

Critical Analysis

The RBI's decision to revise the LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements is a positive development, as it will enhance the transparency and comparability of these disclosures and promote a more stable and resilient banking system in India. However, the revised directions may also pose challenges for commercial banks, particularly smaller banks that may not have the necessary resources or expertise to comply with the enhanced disclosure requirements. For instance, a smaller bank may need to invest in new systems and processes to collect and disclose the required data, which can be a significant burden.

The revised directions may also raise questions about the adequacy of the LCR and NSFR thresholds prescribed by the RBI. The LCR threshold is currently set at 100%, while the NSFR threshold is set at 100%. These thresholds may need to be reviewed and revised in light of changing market conditions and the evolving risk landscape. For example, the RBI may need to consider whether the current thresholds are sufficient to ensure the stability and resilience of the banking system, or whether they need to be adjusted to reflect changing circumstances.

Furthermore, the revised directions may have implications for the regulatory framework for commercial banks in India. The enhanced disclosure requirements may necessitate changes to the regulatory framework, such as the introduction of new guidelines or standards for liquidity risk management. The RBI will need to carefully consider these implications and ensure that the regulatory framework is adapted to support the revised disclosure requirements. For instance, the RBI may need to issue new guidelines on liquidity risk management, which can help to ensure that commercial banks are managing their liquidity risks effectively.

Compliance Implications & Action Points

The revised LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements will have significant compliance implications for commercial banks in India. To ensure compliance with the revised directions, commercial banks will need to review and revise their risk management practices, including their liquidity risk management systems and funding strategies. They will also need to ensure that they have the necessary resources and expertise to comply with the enhanced disclosure requirements.

Here are some key takeaways for practitioners: 1. Review and revise risk management practices to ensure compliance with the revised LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements. 2. Ensure that the necessary resources and expertise are in place to comply with the enhanced disclosure requirements. 3. Consider the implications of the revised directions for funding strategies and liquidity risk management systems. 4. Review and revise internal controls and procedures to ensure that they are adequate and effective. 5. Consider seeking external advice or guidance to ensure compliance with the revised directions and to address any questions or concerns that may arise.

Overall, the revised LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements are a positive development that will promote a more stable and resilient banking system in India. Commercial banks will need to take prompt action to ensure compliance with the revised directions and to address any challenges or implications that may arise. By doing so, they can help to promote a more stable and resilient banking system and support the overall health and stability of the Indian economy.

items.body:
Background & Statutory Framework

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has been empowered under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, to regulate and supervise commercial banks in India. Section 35B of the Banking Regulation Act grants the RBI the authority to issue directions to banking companies on various matters, including governance and management. In exercise of this power, the RBI has issued several directions and guidelines to ensure sound governance practices in commercial banks. One such area of focus has been the remuneration and share-linked instruments for bank employees, which is critical for maintaining a balance between attracting talent and ensuring prudent risk management.

The RBI's governance directions for commercial banks are aimed at promoting transparency, accountability, and fairness in the functioning of these banks. These directions are also aligned with international best practices and guidelines issued by bodies such as the Financial Stability Board (FSB) and the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS). The governance framework for banks in India is also influenced by the Companies Act, 2013, particularly in areas such as board composition, audit committees, and disclosure requirements. Section 178 of the Companies Act, for instance, deals with the disclosure of remuneration of directors and key managerial personnel, which has a bearing on the transparency and accountability of banks' remuneration practices.

Furthermore, the RBI's regulatory framework for banks is supported by various circulars and guidelines that provide detailed instructions on specific aspects of bank governance. For example, the RBI's circular on "Guidelines on Compensation of Whole Time Directors/Chief Executive Officers/Material Risk Takers in Private Sector Banks" outlines the principles for determining the compensation of senior bank executives. These guidelines are designed to ensure that banks' remuneration practices are aligned with their risk management objectives and do not encourage excessive risk-taking.

The Development in Detail

The RBI's Third Amendment Directions, 2026, which come into effect from April 1, 2027, introduce significant changes to the governance directions for commercial banks, particularly in the areas of remuneration and share-linked instruments. The amended directions aim to enhance transparency and accountability in banks' remuneration practices, aligning them with global best practices and the evolving regulatory landscape. The amendments are a response to the changing nature of banking and the need for more robust governance frameworks that can mitigate risks and promote financial stability.

A key aspect of the amended directions is the revision of remuneration disclosure requirements for commercial banks. The RBI has introduced more stringent disclosure norms to ensure that banks provide detailed information about the remuneration of their employees, including whole-time directors, chief executive officers, and material risk takers. This move is expected to enhance transparency and facilitate better oversight by regulators and stakeholders. The amended directions also provide clarity on the composition of remuneration, including the proportion of fixed and variable components, which will help in assessing the alignment of remuneration with banks' long-term goals and risk management objectives.

The amendments also cover share-linked instruments, which are an integral part of the remuneration packages for senior bank executives. The RBI has introduced new guidelines to ensure that these instruments are designed and implemented in a manner that promotes prudent risk management and aligns with the banks' overall strategic objectives. The guidelines are expected to prevent the misuse of share-linked instruments and ensure that they do not encourage excessive risk-taking or short-termism among bank executives. By introducing these changes, the RBI aims to strengthen the governance framework for commercial banks and promote a culture of transparency, accountability, and prudence in the banking sector.

Key Provisions & Impact

The key provisions of the RBI's Third Amendment Directions, 2026, relate to the enhanced disclosure requirements for remuneration, the revised guidelines for share-linked instruments, and the strengthened governance framework for commercial banks. These provisions are expected to have a significant impact on the banking sector, as they will influence the way banks design their remuneration packages, disclose information about executive compensation, and manage risks associated with share-linked instruments. The amendments will also affect the role of bank boards and remuneration committees, which will be required to play a more active role in overseeing remuneration practices and ensuring their alignment with the banks' overall strategy and risk management objectives.

The impact of the amended directions will be felt across the banking sector, with commercial banks required to review and revise their remuneration policies and practices to ensure compliance with the new guidelines. The enhanced disclosure requirements will increase transparency and facilitate better oversight by regulators and stakeholders, which could lead to more informed decision-making and improved governance practices. The revisions to share-linked instruments will help in mitigating risks associated with these instruments and ensuring that they are used in a manner that promotes prudent risk management and long-term sustainability.

The amendments will also have implications for the broader financial sector, as they will influence the way other financial institutions and regulated entities approach remuneration and governance. The RBI's initiative is part of a global trend towards enhancing governance standards and promoting transparency and accountability in the financial sector. By introducing these changes, the RBI is contributing to the development of a more robust and resilient financial system in India, which is better equipped to manage risks and promote financial stability.

Critical Analysis

A critical analysis of the RBI's Third Amendment Directions, 2026, reveals that the amendments are a significant step towards enhancing governance standards in the banking sector. The enhanced disclosure requirements and the revised guidelines for share-linked instruments are designed to promote transparency, accountability, and prudent risk management. However, the effectiveness of these amendments will depend on the manner in which they are implemented and the extent to which banks comply with the new guidelines.

One of the key challenges in implementing the amended directions will be ensuring that banks have the necessary systems and processes in place to comply with the enhanced disclosure requirements. This may require significant investments in technology and human resources, particularly for smaller banks that may not have the same level of resources as their larger counterparts. Additionally, the revised guidelines for share-linked instruments may require banks to rethink their remuneration strategies and ensure that they are aligned with the banks' overall strategic objectives and risk management objectives.

From a legal perspective, the amendments are supported by the RBI's powers under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and are consistent with the broader regulatory framework for banks in India. The amendments are also aligned with international best practices and guidelines issued by bodies such as the FSB and the BCBS. However, the effectiveness of the amendments will depend on the extent to which they are enforced by the RBI and the banks' ability to comply with the new guidelines. The RBI will need to play an active role in monitoring compliance and taking enforcement action where necessary to ensure that the amendments achieve their intended objectives.

Compliance Implications & Action Points

The RBI's Third Amendment Directions, 2026, have significant compliance implications for commercial banks in India. Banks will need to review and revise their remuneration policies and practices to ensure compliance with the new guidelines, which will require significant investments in time, resources, and effort. The following are some key action points for practitioners:

1. Review existing remuneration policies and practices to ensure compliance with the enhanced disclosure requirements and the revised guidelines for share-linked instruments.

2. Develop a plan to implement the necessary changes to remuneration policies and practices, including the introduction of new systems and processes to support the enhanced disclosure requirements.

3. Ensure that the bank's board and remuneration committee are aware of their roles and responsibilities in overseeing remuneration practices and ensuring their alignment with the bank's overall strategy and risk management objectives.

4. Provide training to employees on the new guidelines and the requirements for disclosure and compliance, to ensure that they understand their roles and responsibilities in implementing the amendments.

5. Monitor compliance with the amended directions and take corrective action where necessary, to ensure that the bank is meeting its regulatory obligations and minimizing the risk of enforcement action by the RBI.

items.body:
Background & Statutory Framework

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), as the regulator of commercial banks in India, has the power to issue directions to these banks under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. This provision enables the RBI to exercise control over the banking system and ensure the stability of the financial sector. In recent years, the RBI has been taking steps to strengthen the regulatory framework for commercial banks, including the introduction of new disclosure requirements. The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, are the latest development in this regard, and they have significant implications for the financial disclosure norms of commercial banks.

Under the existing framework, commercial banks are required to disclose certain information about their financial position and performance. This includes details about their liquidity, capital adequacy, and risk management practices. The disclosure requirements are designed to promote transparency and accountability in the banking sector, and to enable stakeholders to make informed decisions. The RBI has been reviewing these requirements periodically, and the Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, reflect the latest changes in this area. It is worth examining the specific provisions of the amendment directions and their impact on the financial disclosure norms of commercial banks.

The Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI Act, 1934, provide the statutory framework for the regulation of commercial banks in India. These laws empower the RBI to issue directions to banks on various matters, including financial disclosure. The RBI has also issued guidelines and circulars from time to time to clarify the disclosure requirements and provide guidance to banks. For example, the RBI's Master Circular on Disclosure in Financial Statements, which is updated annually, provides detailed guidance on the disclosure requirements for commercial banks. The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, need to be seen in the context of this broader regulatory framework.

The Development in Detail

The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, delete the requirements for commercial banks to disclose their Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR), Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR), and remuneration details. The LCR and NSFR are key metrics that indicate a bank's ability to meet its short-term and long-term funding needs. The remuneration disclosure requirement, on the other hand, is intended to promote transparency in the compensation practices of banks. The deletion of these requirements is significant, as it may impact the ability of stakeholders to assess the financial health and risk profile of commercial banks.

The amendment directions are effective from April 1, 2027, which means that commercial banks will not be required to disclose the LCR, NSFR, and remuneration details from the next financial year onwards. This change may have implications for the way banks report their financial performance and position, and may also affect the way stakeholders, including investors and regulators, assess the banks' financial health. The RBI has not provided detailed reasons for the deletion of these requirements, but it is likely that the move is intended to simplify the disclosure framework and reduce the regulatory burden on banks.

The deletion of the LCR and NSFR disclosure requirements may also be seen in the context of the Basel III framework, which emphasizes the importance of liquidity and funding risk management in banks. The RBI has been implementing the Basel III norms in India, and the deletion of these requirements may be part of this broader effort to align the regulatory framework with international standards. However, the implications of this change need to be carefully considered, as it may affect the ability of stakeholders to assess the liquidity and funding risk profile of commercial banks.

Key Provisions & Impact

The key provision of the Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, is the deletion of the LCR, NSFR, and remuneration disclosure requirements. This change will simplify the financial disclosure framework for commercial banks and reduce the regulatory burden on them. However, it may also have implications for the ability of stakeholders to assess the financial health and risk profile of banks. The deletion of the remuneration disclosure requirement, in particular, may be seen as a move to reduce the transparency in the compensation practices of banks.

The impact of the amendment directions will depend on the specific circumstances of each bank. Banks that have a strong track record of disclosing their financial information may not be significantly affected by the change. However, banks that have weaker disclosure practices may face challenges in providing alternative information to stakeholders. The amendment directions may also affect the way banks report their financial performance and position, and may require changes to their financial reporting systems and processes.

From a regulatory perspective, the amendment directions reflect the RBI's ongoing efforts to review and refine the financial disclosure framework for commercial banks. The RBI has been taking steps to simplify the regulatory framework and reduce the compliance burden on banks, while also ensuring that the framework remains effective in promoting transparency and accountability. The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, are part of this broader effort, and their impact will need to be carefully monitored and assessed.

Critical Analysis

The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, raise important questions about the balance between regulatory simplicity and transparency in the banking sector. While the deletion of the LCR, NSFR, and remuneration disclosure requirements may simplify the financial disclosure framework, it may also reduce the ability of stakeholders to assess the financial health and risk profile of commercial banks. The RBI will need to carefully monitor the impact of the amendment directions and consider whether additional measures are needed to promote transparency and accountability in the banking sector.

The amendment directions also highlight the need for a nuanced approach to regulatory reform in the banking sector. The RBI will need to balance the competing demands of simplicity, transparency, and effectiveness in the regulatory framework, and ensure that any changes to the framework are carefully considered and calibrated. The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, are a significant development in this regard, and their impact will need to be carefully assessed and evaluated.

From a legal perspective, the amendment directions are authorized under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, which empowers the RBI to issue directions to banks on various matters, including financial disclosure. The RBI has also issued guidelines and circulars from time to time to clarify the disclosure requirements and provide guidance to banks. The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, are part of this broader regulatory framework, and their impact will need to be considered in the context of the overall framework.

Compliance Implications & Action Points

The Eighth Amendment Directions, 2026, have significant implications for the compliance practices of commercial banks in India. Banks will need to review their financial disclosure frameworks and ensure that they are compliant with the amended requirements. The following are some key action points for practitioners:

1. Review the financial disclosure framework: Banks will need to review their financial disclosure frameworks and ensure that they are compliant with the amended requirements. This will involve assessing the impact of the deletion of the LCR, NSFR, and remuneration disclosure requirements and making any necessary changes to the disclosure framework.

2. Update financial reporting systems: Banks will need to update their financial reporting systems and processes to reflect the changes to the disclosure requirements. This may involve changes to the financial statements, notes to accounts, and other disclosure documents.

3. Provide alternative information: Banks may need to provide alternative information to stakeholders to compensate for the deletion of the LCR, NSFR, and remuneration disclosure requirements. This may involve providing additional disclosures about their liquidity and funding risk profile, or their compensation practices.

4. Monitor regulatory developments: Banks will need to monitor regulatory developments closely and assess the impact of any further changes to the financial disclosure framework. This may involve tracking changes to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI Act, 1934, as well as any guidelines or circulars issued by the RBI.

5. Seek professional advice: Banks may need to seek professional advice to ensure that they are compliant with the amended requirements and to assess the impact of the changes on their financial disclosure frameworks. This may involve consulting with auditors, lawyers, and other experts to ensure that the bank is taking a comprehensive and nuanced approach to compliance.

items.title: Delhi ITAT Allows MakeMyTrip’s Claims on Website Depreciation, AMP & Reimbursements
items.summary: Delhi ITAT upheld relief on 60% website depreciation, payment gateway charges, AMP expenses and US reimbursements, dismissing the Revenue's appeal. The post Delhi ITAT Allows MakeMyTrip’s Claims on Website Depreciation, AMP & Reimbursements appeared first on TaxGuru .
items.body:
Background & Legal Framework

The Income Tax Act, 1961, provides the framework for taxation of income in India. Section 32 of the Act allows depreciation on tangible assets, while Section 37 allows deductions for expenditure incurred for the purpose of business. The Act also provides for allowances and deductions for specific expenses, such as payment gateway charges and advertising, marketing, and promotion (AMP) expenses. In recent years, the tax authorities have been scrutinizing claims related to website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses, particularly in the context of e-commerce businesses.

The Delhi ITAT's decision in the MakeMyTrip case is significant, as it clarifies the tax treatment of website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses. The tribunal's ruling is grounded in the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and is consistent with established precedents. For instance, Section 9(1) of the CGST Act, 2017, provides that any supply of goods or services or both made or agreed to be made by a person in the course or furtherance of business shall be treated as a supply made in the course or furtherance of business. Similarly, Section 145A of the Income Tax Act, 1961, provides for the method of accounting to be followed by a taxpayer.

The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) has also issued circulars and guidelines on the tax treatment of website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses. For example, the CBDT has clarified that website development costs can be depreciated over a period of time, and that payment gateway charges are allowable as a business expense. The tribunal's decision in the MakeMyTrip case is consistent with these guidelines and circulars, and provides further clarity on the tax treatment of these expenses.

Facts of the Case

The MakeMyTrip case involved a dispute between the taxpayer, MakeMyTrip, and the Revenue regarding the tax treatment of website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses. The taxpayer had claimed depreciation on its website at the rate of 60%, and had also claimed deductions for payment gateway charges and AMP expenses. The Revenue had disallowed these claims, and the taxpayer had appealed to the Delhi ITAT.

The facts of the case are significant, as they highlight the complexities of taxing e-commerce businesses. The taxpayer had incurred significant expenses on website development, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses, and had claimed these expenses as deductions. The Revenue had disputed these claims, arguing that they were not allowable as business expenses. The tribunal's decision in the case provides clarity on the tax treatment of these expenses, and is likely to have a significant impact on the taxation of e-commerce businesses in India.

The tribunal's decision is also significant, as it highlights the importance of documentation and record-keeping in tax matters. The taxpayer had maintained detailed records of its expenses, and had provided evidence to support its claims. The tribunal's decision emphasizes the need for taxpayers to maintain accurate and detailed records of their expenses, in order to support their claims and avoid disputes with the tax authorities.

Issue Before the Tribunal

The issue before the tribunal was whether the taxpayer's claims for website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses were allowable as business expenses. The Revenue had argued that these expenses were not allowable, as they were not incurred for the purpose of business. The taxpayer had argued that these expenses were incurred for the purpose of business, and were therefore allowable as deductions.

The tribunal's decision in the case turned on the interpretation of the provisions of the Income Tax Act, 1961, and the CGST Act, 2017. The tribunal had to consider whether the taxpayer's claims for website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses were allowable as business expenses, and whether the Revenue's disallowance of these claims was justified. The tribunal's decision provides clarity on the tax treatment of these expenses, and is likely to have a significant impact on the taxation of e-commerce businesses in India.

The tribunal's decision is also significant, as it highlights the importance of considering the facts and circumstances of each case. The tribunal's decision emphasizes the need for a nuanced approach to taxation, taking into account the specific facts and circumstances of each case. The decision is likely to have a significant impact on the taxation of e-commerce businesses in India, and is likely to be cited as a precedent in future cases.

Arguments & Contentions

The taxpayer had argued that its claims for website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses were allowable as business expenses. The taxpayer had submitted that these expenses were incurred for the purpose of business, and were therefore allowable as deductions. The taxpayer had also submitted that the Revenue's disallowance of these claims was unjustified, and that the tribunal should allow the taxpayer's appeals.

The Revenue had argued that the taxpayer's claims for website depreciation, payment gateway charges, and AMP expenses were not allowable as business expenses. The Revenue had submitted that these expenses were not incurred for the purpose of business, and were therefore not allowable as deductions. The Revenue had also submitted that the tribunal should dismiss the taxpayer's appeals, and uphold the Revenue's disallowance of these claims.

items.title: Pune ITAT Reiterates: BSNL VRS Compensation Is Retrenchment Compensation Exempt under Section 10(10B)
items.summary: ITAT held BSNL VRS-2019 compensation to be retrenchment compensation exempt under Section 10(10B), reversed CIT(A) orders, and allowed the appeals.
